 GM recalls 67,000 EVs over brake issue. Would I still recommend them?
 USA TODAY – Cars Charles Singh , USA TODAY Updated Thu, November 5, 2026 at 11:42 PM UTC Add to Preferred Sources Updated Thu, November 5, 2026 at 11:42 PM UTC General Motors is recalling multiple electric vehicle nameplates across its Chevrolet and Cadillac brands. GM is producing some of the best-selling non-Tesla electric vehicles on the market, so the recall may be concerning to some car buyers.
 Should drivers avoid buying these GM electric vehicles because of the huge recall? Here's what shoppers need to know about the issue affecting more than 67,000 General Motors EVs.
 Which GM EVs are being recalled?
 The recall of 67,380 General Motors electric vehicles affects four nameplates across two brands. A software defect "may cause a temporary loss of braking at low speeds," according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. NHTSA also notes that "normal brake function returns on the next brake press."
 The 2026 Chevrolet Blazer EV SS trim has an EPA-estimated 302 miles of range, according to General Motors. No consumer advisories have been listed on the recall notice thus far. Many of the affected vehicles can be remedied through Over-the-Air (OTA) updates. Owners who have not accepted the applicable terms and conditions must bring their vehicles to an authorized GM dealer or service center for the software updates.
 Models impacted by recall
 2023-2027 Cadillac Lyriq
 2025 Cadillac Celestiq
 2026-2027 Cadillac Vistiq
 2024-2027 Chevrolet Blazer EV
 Advertisement Advertisement These four nameplates play a huge role in the company's electrification strategy. If you own one of these GM electric vehicles, don't fret. The recall isn't as dangerous as it may seem. However, owners should address it as quickly as possible to avoid mishaps.
 Is the GM EV braking issue a cause for concern?
 The braking issue isn't a major concern because it typically occurs only under very specific low-speed conditions, such as when a vehicle is turning sharply and hits depressions or bumps. Braking is immediately restored after pressing the brake pedal a second time.
 Female mechanic working under a car lifted on a hydraulic lift, inspecting brakes in a professional car repair shop Furthermore, the minor software glitch can be resolved quickly through an update. Owners should still address the recall immediately to avoid any potential accidents related to the braking issue.
 Would I still recommend these GM EVs?
 General Motors has made huge strides in the electric vehicle space in recent years with models like the Chevrolet Bolt and Chevrolet Equinox. Since GM is recalling the four electric vehicles over a relatively minor software issue, should you still consider them?
 The Chevy Blazer EV starts at $45,000, making it accessible to most average car buyers. I would recommend the Blazer EV because it's spacious, has plenty of driving range (312 miles) and doesn't break the bank. 2027 Blazer EV models also come with a North American Charging Standard (NACS) port for Direct Current (DC) charging with Tesla Superchargers.
 Advertisement Advertisement Cadillac's Lyriq ($59,400) is a strong contender in the luxury midsize two-row electric SUV segment because it has a luxurious cabin and a strong value proposition. The Cadillac Vistiq ($77,500) on the other hand, is outshined by models like the Rivian R1S and Kia EV9 GT-Line.
 I wouldn't recommend the Cadillac Celestiq to drivers because of its incredibly high price (nearly $400,000). Ultimately, GM's recall isn't a reason for car buyers to avoid the company's EVs since it's a minor issue that can be easily fixed.
 Charles Singh is an Autos Connect Reporter for The Tennessean, part of the USA TODAY Network. Contact him at [email protected]
